story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Lakshay. Raveen and I built Cerulion, an open-source Rust robotics runtime that deterministically replays recorded multi-process runs against new code and runs existing ROS 2 nodes unmodified. Repo: https://github.com/cerulion-inc/cerulion

During my MIT PhD in off-road autonomy, a robot with two lidars and six cameras had too much latency between ROS processes. ROS 2's loaned messages need POD data, which rules out the standard sensor types like Image and PointCloud2. We ended up using a single process, which is very brittle.

And when it broke, I couldn't reproduce the heisenbug reliably. ROS bags record messages, not which inputs callbacks consumed or in what order, so replaying them doesn't reproduce execution.

Cerulion records messages, per-input reads and scheduler traces in standard MCAP. `bag play --resim all --verify` re-executes your native nodes on the recorded clock and compares outputs byte-for-byte or within tolerances. Exit 0 matches, 1 names the first divergent topic/frame, 6 means schedule divergence, and `--report` writes the verdict for CI. The trace can show LiDAR frame 47 read instead of 46. Replay uses an isolated shared-memory namespace, safe beside live graphs, and eligible ROS 2 processes replay individually.

Everything else feeds that loop, in the order data moves:

1. Run. Dependency-ordered scheduling with period/data/sync triggers, deadlines, backpressure, parallel same-level nodes and profile-based partitioning. Processes free-run without barriers and still replay deterministically. Live runs pause/resume, and UMWAIT/WFE parks idle consumers. Rust nodes (Python via source build) use a compiler-stable ABI, and macros reject wall-clock reads and thread spawns at compile time.

ROS 2: prebuilt Jazzy/Lyrical `rmw_cerulion` runs nodes unmodified in the same graph (11.12 µs median at 1 MiB loaned, MoveIt 2 unchanged). `LD_PRELOAD` gives them shared-memory loans through `std::vector`/`std::string`. `ros2 attach` bridges live DDS robots, and `ros2 migrate` rewrites C++ publish sites for loaning.

2. Move. iceoryx2 shared memory with no serialization, no payload copy and no payload-sized allocation, variable-length messages included. A 1 MiB `sensor_msgs/Image` round trip between two processes takes 4.08 µs median / 7.38 µs p99 (under 2x) with recording on, versus 10.95 ms for stock ROS 2 Jazzy. p50 stays flat from 64 B to 16 MiB.

3. Capture. At that round-trip latency we can afford always-on or event-based bagging. Flashback keeps ~30 seconds in memory and saves it automatically on crashes, topic stalls or declared incidents.

4. Reach. Account-paired robots and desks find each other without addresses. Pub/sub is authenticated and on demand, with signed grants the robot verifies offline. Iroh QUIC hole-punches or relays, and opening the LAN up routes through mDNS and QUIC/TLS 1.3. Remote topics mirror into local shared memory.

5. Diagnose. `cerulion doctor` finds host problems and names the fix. Hindsight (early access) gives coding agents recording analysis over MCP.

Quickstart: run obstacle avoidance, record, change a controller constant, verify the divergence. The CLI needs a free account, used for automatic robot pairing. Everything runs on Linux (x86_64/ARM64), macOS and Android (JNI), with more platforms coming.

We'd love to hear your feedback! If you run ROS 2 on a real robot, point this at your stack and tell us what breaks.

Docs: https://docs.cerulion.com

Site: https://cerulion.com

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Dennis and I wanted to share what I've been working on. Mudroom is a unified inbox for SaaS teams that have support requests scattered across platforms.

Here's a quick demo: https://youtu.be/GFafCfwqNf4

As an engineer, one of the things often frustrated me is how I had to context switch between a task that I'm working on to a support request that required engineering investigation. Often they revolve around digging through logs, customer profiles, and billing and we believe agents are well equipped to handle data gathering.

We're strong believers that customers want to interact with Humans instead of AI for their support tickets so our philosophy revolves around empowering humans rather than replacing them.

We're still early and so we're valuing feedback more than revenue. If you want to try us out, let me know and I'll personally onboard your team. Would love to hear what you think so feel free to leave a message comment :)

story_text.value:
I know you've already seen the "new" github design for the PR UI, it barely fixes anything and I've been trying to fix all of github's issues one at a time.

I eventually built a client to replace it, fully driven on the github APIs, fixes all the bugs and pain points and makes it easy to manage PRs and feedback comments like Slack threads.

Every review comment lands in one inbox with unread state, like Slack threads. you open a thread and the code it’s about is right above it, which you can expand for more context, and save filters as views (e.g. only unresolved threads or per repo threads, etc).

try it on web or desktop: https://pyor.review/download

1 min demo: https://youtu.be/aejLtTAT5Og

I’m picking what to fix next from replies here.

story_text.value:
I created Easy Dashcam to ditch an app called viidure which it's super slow and request gps permission and does no allow background downloads. The camera name in the box is Reddot Dashcam and in About this camera reports 1084-w90-WIFI-7789 and firmware 20250306 V1.0. The app connects over the camera’s local Wi-Fi connection. It can show live video and audio, browse and download recordings, play them back, and change camera settings. The camera protocol was reverse-engineered because I couldn’t find any standard for this type of camera

I’d like to support more cameras eventually, specially cheap Chinese models. I’m looking for owners who can help test whether their cameras use the same GPSOCKET protocol or require a different implementation or people who would like to contribute.

Source and demo: https://github.com/juanmespina/EasyDashcam

story_text.value:
Hey y'all, I'm Nick. I wanted to share a side project I started sometime last month.

I really enjoy incremental games (like Cookie Clicker, Scritchy Scratchy, etc.) and wondered if I could get a coding agent to build a new one every day that I'd actually want to play.

So I built an incremental game development harness with Claude Code. The first games were pretty rough, but I found that adding a few architectural invariants and automated playtesting around things like pacing and progression made a surprisingly big difference. They're now pretty fun most days.

My partner and I have been playing and talking about the games each day, and after some encouragement from a teammate, I figured I'd share the experiment with the HN community.

The code is available here: https://github.com/nickdirienzo/incremendle

It's AGPL in part because it uses Strudel for music generation. I've also tried to be thoughtful about crediting the artists whose work inspires the games.

Would love to hear what you think of this silly experiment!

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I work on multi-modal sensing for robotics.

We built DRS-VPT to estimate a camera's 6-DoF pose in a 3D map from a single photo and a 3D point cloud, without an initial guess or known camera intrinsics.

The interesting part is generalisation: the same model works across driving LiDAR scans (KITTI, nuScenes), iPhone photos in indoor scans, and SFM maps.

We provide the code, model and weights, but you can also try it out at https://huggingface.co/spaces/fulkast/drs-vpt-demo

Happy to answer questions about the method or its limitations!

story_text.value:
Hey HN! I am Harsh, been developing software for quite sometime now. Since agents came into my local SD workflow I had been facing a bottleneck. Event though agents are great in working parallelly, testing their changes and iterating is a pain. (Brain, storage & memory overhead)

We all use Git worktrees to code in parallel. But how do we test those changes? Still linearly. Or patched up multi-environment setup.

And what if you have multiple microservices in an application? How do you test different combinations?

I am building Headwig to help me with this.

It lets me run multiple agents on my app, isolate their changes across services, and test and iterate on each one independently, even while other agents are working, without the storage overhead of duplicating workspaces for every task.

I've been using it for my own webapp, and I want you guys to look at the workflow and see if it makes sense and give me any suggestions or feedback. https://harsh-kr-jha.github.io/headwig/

story_text.value:
I am pharmacist, in France and I order directly from more than a hundred suppliers. Most orders are a web form, an email or a phone call .

I built a buying agent for my pharmacy and the problem came fast: there is nobody to talk to on the other side. A supplier has a sales rep with a mailbox, sometimes an ERP.

The idea is PharmA2A. It's based on the A2A protocol. PharmA2A says what they say. Five messages, each one a JSON Schema: supplier sheet, order , acknowledgement line by line, state of the shelf, follow-up.

Some rules are strict. The order never has a pharmacy's price in it. Nothing is invented. And a message that says nothing is not a confirmation. One of the first answers we got from a sales rep was "looks good to me :)". Is that a confirmation? We had to decide.

In the repo: the spec (CC0), a sample supplier agent in about a hundred lines of Python, an email bridge for suppliers who only have a mailbox, and a demo pharmacy.

It has carried real orders since October, in my own pharmacy. No supplier runs its own agent yet.

I would like your opinion: is an A2A profile extension the right shape for this? And what would a supplier's IT team need to plug an ERP into it?

title.value: Show HN: PharmA2A, an open protocol for pharmacy-to-supplier orders on A2A

story_text.value:
Hey HN! We're Alireza and Majid building Leeroo (https://leeroo.com/). Previously we’ve built AI systems for products with millions of users, including at LinkedIn and Meta. We’re now focusing on building AI systems for enterprise data. Today, we're open-sourcing Kapso (https://github.com/Leeroo-AI/kapso), an engine that runs experiments, deploys the best solution, and learns from every run.

The nature of data work is iterative: investigate, form hypotheses, experiment, and improve based on what you learn. This bottom-up process is the only way to deliver meaningful outcomes quickly in large, messy enterprise data environments. Consultants gathering context in meetings or teams defining a business ontology upfront to fit into the data has no chance of execution, in quarters and sometimes years. An AI-native system should automate this process, compounding learning to each new investigation and implementation.

For instance, one of our enterprise projects was moving a company off its old data estate onto a lakehouse with more than 30 source-system families, thousands of tables and transformations, and hundreds of BI reports. No individual or AI agent knew how that data estate was connected and operated. The only way to learn it was to investigate the company's repos, dbt models, documentation, and data itself and propose hypotheses about the estate, run experiments, and learn from them, until we understand how each system behaves and under which conditions.

The iterative work goes beyond understanding how data and systems fit together, and the business operations. Building useful software is iterative too. Whether you’re optimizing a warehouse, building a lakehouse pipeline or predicting churn, you need to run experiments and learn what works best in that environment. As you deliver more projects, that know-how compounds, similar in principle to RL. RAGing documentation has little value until it has been tried in a specific environment and the consequences are learned. As with human engineering work, experimentation and learning should happen in a sandbox.

We built Kapso for this kind of work, you give it an objective and success criteria, and it works towards an optimum solution that can be deployed on your stack.

You can view a video walkthrough here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W4FHlza1fRs

Here’s how it works…

Kapso has a bank of lessons that are induced or deduced from the past experiments, and each carries a credence score, conditions on where it applies, and the evidence behind it. For each new experiment, an ideation module proposes ideas considering the earlier lessons, re-ranks them by expected return against the budget each would use, and sends the top-ranked ones to the implementor. Because the bank keeps learning from the past experiments in that environment, the proposed ideas are better suited to it than generic hypotheses from an LLM or RAG. Also, results of each experiment are verified by a verifier module that no experiment can access and cheat. As we’ve found when building such systems, sometimes the success criteria and evaluation tests need to be evolved. The experimentation modules can propose updates to the metrics and criteria for the verifier to approve or reject.

After each run, learn() updates the bank of lessons’ scores and boundaries using the evidence from that run. Changes to the bank can also be A/B tested by running otherwise identical builds with the previous and updated banks. The bank is built on git, so you can share your experience with others, list the banks available to you, and update them (`kapso experience share/list/update` in CLI). The system is model-agnostic and coding-agent-agnostic.

kapso.deploy(solution, target_stack) follows the same workflow, runs a shorter experimentation loop to adapt the best solution to the target stack (e.g. Docker, Modal, BentoCloud, LangGraph). Every domain has a harness to start from, you can write your own domain harness with /kapso:harness in the plugin or through CLI (kapso harness new <name>), and compound over that by running experimentations.

We ran it on some public benchmarks and live competitions, with the following results…

- Predictive modelling on relational databases: first on RelBench, Kumo AI (now Nvidia) and Stanford's benchmark, ahead of the best tabular foundation model (https://star-project.stanford.edu/relbench/leaderboard/). This shows that keeping the learning in the harness-level can beat foundational table models. Updating a bank of lessons costs far less than retraining a tabular foundation model.

- ML Engineering: First on OpenAI's MLE-bench at submission, still among the top open-source systems (https://github.com/openai/mle-bench/pull/107).

- AI competitions: ahead of the best agent the ALE-Bench authors at Sakana AI reported, and running autonomously at the live International Olympiad in AI 2026, above all 471 human contestants and in the top three AI systems (https://ioai-official.org/ai-models-track/ioai%c2%b2-2026-re...).

We have a public bank for ML and Data at Leeroopedia (https://leeroopedia.com/): around 100k pages extracted by experimenting on papers and repos, about 6M requests a month, about 28% from AI agents.

If you are at a growing company with a complex data estate across multiple systems and functions, and your data and AI team is stretched, we would love to help!

https://github.com/Leeroo-AI/kapso
